Hyphae fixed together as if with glue Hyphal outgrowth which makes a connection between two neighbouring cells of a hypha, and contains two septa. Hyphae of finite length having very distinct and characteristic shapes, occurring on the mantle surface or on hyphal cords. A group of tissues situated between the vascular system and the epidermis. Branching, often successive, into two reasonably equal segments. Hyphae that grow outward from the ectomycorrhizal mantle and connect it to the surrounding soil. Primary mature tissue, generally consisting of a single layer of cells, that covers plant organs. Cell walls of the swollen hyphae, capable of absorbing considerable amounts of water or potassium hydroxide solution. Net-like structure between cortical cells formed by hyphae growing intercellularly. Hyphae produced by various mechanisms, growing more or less parallel to one another and remaining united over a certain distance; may exhibit varying degrees of organization. Section made perpendicular to the length of the root to show the epidermis, cortex, and central cylinder. Hyphae arranged more or less densely around the root The hyphae of the mantle are embedded in a gelatinous substance. Multiple ectomycorrhizae connected by axes to form branched clusters, sometimes with characteristic shapes. Mycorrhiza from the apex proper to the next branching point. Cell with a thin primary wall, large vacuole, few intercellular spaces, and a vacuole occupying more than 80% of the cell. Observation of the mantle surface at sufficiently high magnifications, frequently used to recognize and characterize different types of mantle surfaces. Structure composed of hyphae that are more or less parallel or irregularly arranged, generally still recognizable as individual hyphae. Mantle hyphae, in surface view or in section, arranged so closely that they resemble parenchymatous tissue. Type of trichome on the root epidermis, an outgrowth of an epidermal cell, involved in the absorption of soil solution. The outermost part of the mantle as observed from the surface. Agerer, 1987, Apezzato da Glória & Carmello-Guerreiro, 2012.
